left.title: Hey there, welcome to my world!
left.subtitle: I'm Lucas, a computer science student about to graduate from a French engineering school, and I'm looking for my first role as a DevOps or Cloud engineer. What I love is the whole life of an application: building it, automating it, shipping it and keeping it running. Fun fact: this very portfolio is served from a server I configured entirely as code!

right.title: My portfolio — my playground
right.subtitle: Explore the projects that shape who I am as a developer:

type-of-projects.name: Cloud & DevOps
type-of-projects.description: This is where I feel most at home. I built a small cloud provider from scratch in Rust to understand what really happens under the hood, and I run my own VPS entirely described as code with Terraform, Ansible and GitHub Actions: every project here deploys itself on a simple git push. Docker, CI/CD, Linux, monitoring… DevOps isn’t just a buzzword for me, it’s how I think and build.

type-of-projects.name: Full-Stack
type-of-projects.description: Knowing how an application is built makes me better at running it. I enjoy designing clean REST APIs and lively frontends, mostly with Spring Boot, Next.js and React, and I especially love making tools for real people, like a no-code studio for a streamer’s Twitch bot.

type-of-projects.name: AI Experiments
type-of-projects.description: I also explore AI through small but impactful projects, from a RAG system generating law exam questions to machine learning models served through an API. It isn’t my main focus, but I love how it can give an application superpowers.

projects.title: ByLucas Self-Hosting Platform
projects.long_title: My Own Production Server, Fully Described as Code
projects.subtitle: Terraform, Ansible and GitHub Actions powering every *.bylucas.eu project on a single VPS.
projects.short_description: Infrastructure as code for my personal VPS: DNS with Terraform, server setup with Ansible, and automatic deployment of every project on git push.
projects.non_technical_description: Instead of relying on hosting platforms, I rent a small server and host my projects myself, including this portfolio. Everything lives under the bylucas.eu domain, with a home page that leads to my portfolio and to a private monitoring dashboard. The whole server is described in configuration files, so if it ever disappears I can rebuild it identically with a couple of commands. And every time I push code to GitHub, the matching website updates itself within a minute.
projects.technical_description: The platform is split into three layers. Terraform, with the OVH provider, manages the DNS records (bylucas.eu and the *.bylucas.eu wildcard pointing to the VPS). An Ansible playbook of a dozen roles turns a blank Ubuntu VPS into a production server: SSH hardening, UFW firewall, fail2ban, unattended upgrades, swap, nginx with Let's Encrypt certificates, PostgreSQL with daily backups, Docker (Warp10 and a Minecraft server), and an app-deploy role that generates a systemd service, an nginx vhost, a .env file and a TLS certificate for every project declared in a single variables file. Secrets are encrypted with ansible-vault. Finally, a reusable GitHub Actions workflow, shared by all project repositories, builds the code, ships it with rsync over SSH and restarts the right service. The landing page itself is a Next.js app exported as static files and served directly by nginx.
projects.global_summary: This project is where all my DevOps knowledge comes together in real production. Adding a new website now takes one entry in a YAML file and a git push: Ansible prepares the server, GitHub Actions delivers the code, and nginx serves it over HTTPS. It taught me infrastructure as code, Linux server security and how to design a deployment pipeline that stays simple to maintain.

projects.title: My Cloud
projects.long_title: A Mini Cloud Provider Built From Scratch in Rust
projects.subtitle: Reverse proxy, container orchestrator, object storage, metrics and VPN, with no framework.
projects.short_description: A small cloud provider written from scratch in Rust: containers, object storage, metrics, an encrypted VPN and a Next.js dashboard.
projects.non_technical_description: Services like AWS or Google Cloud let you run programs and store files on someone else's servers. I wanted to understand what really happens behind the scenes, so I built a tiny version of one myself. From a web dashboard you can create and launch isolated programs (containers), upload and download files, and watch the machine's CPU and memory in real time. Every piece is small enough to be read in one sitting, which makes it a good way to learn how a real cloud works.
projects.technical_description: The project is a Cargo workspace of independent Rust binaries that talk plain HTTP/1.1 over TCP. There is no web framework and no async runtime: the HTTP parser, the routing and the thread-per-connection model are hand-written. A reverse proxy acts as the single entry point, checks a bearer token on write requests and forwards traffic by URL prefix. The orchestrator stores containers in a JSON file, launches processes inside an OverlayFS (copy-on-write, like Docker image layers) with cgroups limits, and runs a reconciliation loop that restarts crashed containers every 5 seconds. The storage service is an S3-style key/value store protected against path traversal, the observability service reads host and per-process metrics from /proc, and a point-to-point VPN tunnels a TUN interface over UDP with ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption. A Next.js 16 / React 19 / Tailwind 4 dashboard sits on top and polls the API.
projects.global_summary: My Cloud is an educational deep dive into the building blocks of cloud computing. Rewriting an HTTP server, a container runtime, an object store and an encrypted tunnel without any framework taught me a lot about Linux internals (OverlayFS, cgroups, /proc, TUN devices), concurrency in Rust and network protocols, the same things that big cloud providers hide behind their APIs.

projects.title: VPS Monitoring Dashboard
projects.long_title: A Private Dashboard to Watch and Repair My Server
projects.subtitle: Live status, logs, restarts and TLS certificates for every hosted project.
projects.short_description: A Next.js dashboard that monitors my VPS and its services, streams live logs and can restart a service or reissue a certificate.
projects.non_technical_description: When you host several websites on your own server, you need a way to know if everything is running fine. This dashboard shows at a glance how much memory and disk the server uses, which websites are up or down, and the latest warnings or errors for each of them. If something breaks, I can restart a website or fix its security certificate in one click, without opening a terminal.
projects.technical_description: The dashboard is a Next.js 16 server application whose API routes act as a thin layer over Linux commands: systemctl for service status and memory, journalctl for logs, docker inspect for containers, df and /proc/meminfo for host metrics, and certbot for certificates. Live logs are streamed to the browser with Server-Sent Events from a journalctl -f process that is killed as soon as the client disconnects. It has no database: the list of services comes from JSON manifests generated by Ansible. Security is layered: nginx basic auth and rate limiting in front, commands run with execFile (no shell, so no injection), every service name is checked against the manifests, and root actions are limited to a dedicated sudoers allow-list.
projects.global_summary: A small but practical tool that closes the loop of my self-hosting platform: after deploying, I can also observe and fix. Building it was a good exercise in safely exposing system administration through a web interface, with a strong focus on least privilege and input validation.

projects.title: Pokédex Cloud Platform
projects.long_title: A CI/CD-Powered Pokédex Deployed on Google Cloud
projects.subtitle: Microservices, Cloud Run, Cloud SQL, and automated pipelines.
projects.short_description: A cloud-powered Pokédex with CI/CD pipelines deploying React and Spring Boot services.
projects.non_technical_description: An online Pokédex: you can browse Pokémon, sort them by number, type or name, and look at their details. We built it as a team of three, and the whole thing runs on Google Cloud.
projects.technical_description: The app is split into two services living in separate repositories: a React front-end and a Spring Boot API, backed by a MySQL database on Cloud SQL. Cloud Build pipelines deploy both services to Cloud Run, and Docker Compose let us run the whole stack locally. My part was mostly the cloud side: setting up the GCP infrastructure and the CI/CD pipelines, plus some help on the front-end.
projects.global_summary: My first real hands-on project with a public cloud. Wiring Cloud Build, Cloud Run and Cloud SQL together showed me how a deployment pipeline works from end to end, from a git push to a running service.

projects.title: CatBut 3
projects.long_title: A Modular Twitch Bot With Its Own No-Code Studio
projects.subtitle: Third version of my Twitch bot: plugins, live events, and a visual editor for streamers.
projects.short_description: A plugin-based Twitch bot reacting to chat and stream events, configurable through a friendly local web studio instead of JSON.
projects.non_technical_description: CatBut started as a small bot for a streamer friend and kept growing. This third version can greet viewers, run mini-games like duels, trivia and roulette, keep a loyalty points system, thank people for follows, subs and raids, play sounds on stream, show the song currently playing on Spotify and even move the streamer's virtual avatar. Everything used to be set up in a technical configuration file, so I built CatBut Studio: a cosy web interface where the streamer creates commands step by step, picks from templates and previews the chat message before saving, without writing a single line of code.
projects.technical_description: The bot runs on Node.js and uses the Twurple libraries to connect to Twitch chat, the Helix API and EventSub over WebSocket, with OAuth tokens refreshed automatically. Every chat command and Twitch event is mapped to a handler, either built-in or provided by a plugin; the plugin loader validates each plugin and gives it its own persisted storage. Thirteen plugins cover counters, points, rate limiting, giveaways, duels, trivia, roulette, shoutouts, scheduled messages, OBS scene control through obs-websocket, sounds, VTube Studio and Spotify. A template formatter injects variables such as the sender, target or event data, permissions are checked per command, and user input is sanitised with a protection for the broadcaster. The configuration lives in a single JSON file with schema validation. CatBut Studio is a local HTTP server written in TypeScript (run natively by Node 24) with a vanilla JS front-end bundled by esbuild: it exposes a validated REST API over the config, detects conflicts and references between commands, and is covered by Node test runner tests.
projects.global_summary: CatBut 3 turns a hobby bot into a real product: a plugin architecture that makes new features cheap to add, real-time integration with Twitch and streaming tools, and a no-code interface designed for a non-technical user. It is the project where I think the most about the person on the other side of the screen.

projects.title: Auth API
projects.long_title: A Spring Boot Authentication API with JWT and Refresh Tokens
projects.subtitle: Sign-up, login, logout and session refresh, built in three days.
projects.short_description: An authentication API with JWT access tokens, refresh tokens, a token blacklist and a CI/CD pipeline.
projects.non_technical_description: Almost every website needs a safe way to sign up, log in and log out. This project is exactly that building block: an API that creates accounts, checks who you are and keeps your session alive without asking for your password every few minutes, while keeping out anyone who shouldn't get in.
projects.technical_description: Built with Spring Boot, Spring Security and PostgreSQL. Users receive a short-lived JWT access token and a refresh token to renew it, and tokens are blacklisted on logout so they can't be reused. The code follows the usual layers (models, DTOs with request validation, repositories, services, controllers) with a dedicated security configuration. Unit tests cover the core features, Docker Compose sets up the environment, and a CI/CD pipeline builds and deploys it automatically.
projects.global_summary: I built it in three days to really understand token-based authentication with Spring Security. It's now a building block I can reuse in any backend that needs proper user management.

projects.title: Data Battle IA Pau
projects.long_title: An AI-Driven Platform to Generate Law Exam Questions
projects.subtitle: Semi-finalist – 2-week AI competition.
projects.short_description: A full RAG system generating law exam questions from 200 complex documents.
projects.non_technical_description: The goal was to help law students revise. We gave the platform around 200 documents (lessons, past exams and their corrections) and it generates multiple-choice questions from them, so students can practise on the actual course material.
projects.technical_description: Under the hood it's a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) pipeline. We cleaned the documents by hand, split them into sentences and turned them into embeddings for semantic search, so the generated questions stay grounded in the course content. A Python/FastAPI service generates the questions and answers, a Spring Boot API handles user accounts, JWT authentication and storage, PostgreSQL keeps the generated questions, and the front-end is built with SvelteKit. I worked on cleaning the dataset, generating the embeddings, authentication and several backend services.
projects.global_summary: Two intense weeks of competition, ending in the semi-finals. It was my first RAG system, and running two backends side by side taught me a lot about splitting responsibilities between services.

projects.title: FastAPI Wine Intelligence
projects.long_title: A Machine Learning API Predicting Wine Quality and Composition
projects.subtitle: Two ML models, full CRUD, and retraining through the API.
projects.short_description: A FastAPI service hosting two ML models capable of predicting wine quality or chemical composition.
projects.non_technical_description: This API is built around a dataset of about 1,600 wines. You can browse and edit the wines, predict the quality of a wine from its chemical analysis, or do the reverse and get the typical composition of a wine of a given quality.
projects.technical_description: Written in Python with FastAPI, organised in routers, with request authentication and full CRUD on the wines. Two RandomForestRegressor models handle the predictions: one estimates quality from chemical features, the other estimates the expected composition from a target quality. The dataset holds 1,597 entries, and the models can be retrained with a simple API call.
projects.global_summary: A small project, but a complete loop: data, training, serving and retraining, all behind one API. A good first step into putting machine learning models into production.

projects.title: CatLendar
projects.long_title: A Cosy Stream Planner for a Twitch Streamer
projects.subtitle: A private calendar and to-do list, self-hosted with PostgreSQL.
projects.short_description: A cute, passcode-protected calendar and notepad built with Next.js and PostgreSQL to plan streams and tasks.
projects.non_technical_description: CatLendar is a small planning app I made for a streamer. On a single page you can see the whole month, add streams, collabs and special events with their own colours, and keep a to-do list of things to prepare next to the calendar. The design is soft and playful to match the streamer's universe, and the app is protected by a simple access code so it stays private.
projects.technical_description: Built with Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19 and Tailwind CSS 4. The data lives in PostgreSQL (categories, events and tasks tables) accessed through the pg driver from server-side API routes only, with a shared connection pool reused across hot reloads. Access is protected by a passcode: the login route compares it in constant time and sets an httpOnly, SameSite=strict cookie containing a SHA-256 hash, which a Next.js proxy (edge middleware) checks with Web Crypto on every request. The calendar handles multi-day events, coloured categories and month navigation, and the notepad separates pending and completed tasks. The app is deployed on my VPS at catlendar.bylucas.eu with the shared GitHub Actions workflow and a systemd service generated by Ansible.
projects.global_summary: A focused full-stack app built for a real user: clean data model, lightweight but solid authentication, and a design that is fun to use every day. It is also one of the first projects running in production on my own self-hosting platform.

projects.title: Corpauration Marketplace
projects.long_title: A Full Marketplace for a School Association
projects.subtitle: A product catalogue, authentication and an admin dashboard, built in two months.
projects.short_description: An online shop for a school association: students browse and buy products, admins manage the catalogue, prices and stock.
projects.non_technical_description: The school association needed an online shop. Students could browse the catalogue and buy items, while the association's admins had their own interface to add products, change prices and keep track of stock.
projects.technical_description: The API is written in Kotlin with Spring Boot and PostgreSQL, and the front-end in Vue.js with Vuetify. It covers authentication, admin-only features and full product management, with a layered backend (models, DTOs, repositories, controllers, configuration). It took about two months from start to finish.
projects.global_summary: An application used by students at my school, and my first project with a real admin side. It showed me how much thought goes into permissions and data management once other people depend on your app.

projects.title: Landes Gonflables
projects.long_title: Professional Showcase Website for a Local Business
projects.subtitle: First professional experience — delivered in 3 weeks.
projects.short_description: The website of a company renting inflatable structures, with a gallery, prices and a contact form.
projects.non_technical_description: Landes Gonflables rents out inflatable structures for events. During my internship I built their website so customers could see the inflatables, check the prices and get in touch. It went live, served real customers and helped the company become more visible online.
projects.technical_description: Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no framework. The company had no web team, so I handled everything myself, from the page structure and the gallery to the deployment on IONOS.
projects.global_summary: My first professional project, delivered in three weeks. Being the only developer meant making every decision myself and working with a real client, which taught me a lot.

projects.title: Scorejam 2025 – Roll a Die
projects.long_title: A Fast-Paced Unity Game Built in 3 Days for Scorejam 2025
projects.subtitle: Ranked 21/131 – A dice-based roguelike inspired by Binding of Isaac.
projects.short_description: A Unity game made in three days for a game jam: you play a cursed die trying to escape hell, chased by enemies, with bonus rolls between rooms.
projects.non_technical_description: You play a living die stuck in a hellish maze full of enemies. After clearing each room, you roll a die to win a random bonus, so no two runs are the same. The whole game has a casino-in-hell vibe.
projects.technical_description: Made with Unity and C# by a team of four in three days: two developers, a graphic artist and a sound designer. Enemies use NavMesh pathfinding to chase the player through the rooms. On the development side, we wrote the movement controller, the enemy behaviours, the bonus system and the animation handling.
projects.global_summary: Shipping a whole game in three days with four people is a great lesson in scoping and teamwork. We finished 21st out of 131 entries.

projects.title: catTree
projects.long_title: A Themed Link-in-Bio Page for a Twitch Streamer
projects.subtitle: A hand-made Linktree alternative with an animated night sky and a secret spooky mode.
projects.short_description: A custom link-in-bio page for a streamer, with a starry animated background and a switchable 'Grim' theme showcasing the streamer's team.
projects.non_technical_description: Many content creators use a single page that gathers all their links: Twitch, Discord, TikTok, YouTube and so on. Instead of a generic service, I designed one that looks like the streamer's world, with a cosy starry sky and clouds. A 'My team' button transforms the whole page into a darker, spooky version where the streamers of the team appear around the card, each with a link to their channel.
projects.technical_description: Built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS 4. A theme context and a typed theme system drive every colour through CSS variables, so switching to the Grim theme only changes variables and fonts (Baloo 2 and Creepster, loaded once with next/font) without remounting components. The team members are always in the DOM and animated in with opacity transitions for a smooth switch. The animated starry sky is its own component, icons come from lucide-react, and the layout adapts to mobile, where most visitors arrive from social apps. It is deployed on my VPS through the shared GitHub Actions workflow.
projects.global_summary: A small project, but a good exercise in theming and front-end polish: a design system with typed themes, smooth transitions and attention to the mobile experience, made for a real content creator.

projects.title: Google Wrapper
projects.long_title: A CI/CD Demonstration Project Mimicking Old Google
projects.subtitle: A playful search interface with an intentionally broken keyboard mechanic.
projects.short_description: A fun React project deployed via Docker and CI/CD, recreating old Google but with a twist: the keyboard behaves incorrectly.
projects.non_technical_description: It looks like the Google homepage of the early 2000s, but typing is a challenge: each key press cycles through the letters, and you have to wait before moving on to the next one. It's annoying on purpose, and that's the joke.
projects.technical_description: A React app packaged with Docker, built and deployed automatically by a GitHub Actions workflow. The search field doesn't read the key you press: it increments the current letter in code and only moves to the next character after a short delay. The real point of the project was the CI/CD pipeline.
projects.global_summary: Built in a single day as a CI/CD exercise. A silly idea, but a good excuse to set up a complete build-and-deploy pipeline from scratch.

projects.title: Twitch Chat Bot
projects.long_title: The First Version of My Twitch Bot
projects.subtitle: Where CatBut started: custom commands and live reactions in a Twitch chat.
projects.short_description: The first version of my Twitch bot: custom chat commands and automatic reactions to make streams more interactive.
projects.non_technical_description: A bot that lives in a streamer's Twitch chat. Viewers type commands to trigger messages or actions, and the bot reacts on its own to what happens on stream, which makes the chat livelier and more fun.
projects.technical_description: Written in JavaScript and connected to Twitch with OAuth tokens. It parses chat commands, reacts to real-time events and builds dynamic replies. I kept it modular so new commands could be added quickly.
projects.global_summary: A side project that grew a little with every stream, and later turned into CatBut 3, a full rewrite with plugins and a visual editor.

projects.title: Chuck Norris Angular App
projects.long_title: A Joke-Fetching Angular App Using the Chuck Norris Public API
projects.subtitle: First exploration of Angular HttpClient, Observables, and BehaviorSubjects.
projects.short_description: A small Angular interface that fetches Chuck Norris jokes with filtering options.
projects.non_technical_description: A small website that shows Chuck Norris jokes on demand. Pick a category and get a new joke in one click.
projects.technical_description: The app calls the ChuckNorris.io API with Angular's HttpClient. Observables and BehaviorSubjects keep the state in sync, so the page updates as soon as a new joke arrives.
projects.global_summary: Built in a day to get comfortable with calling an API and handling reactive data in Angular.

projects.title: Angular Memory Game
projects.long_title: A Celest-Themed Memory Game Built with Angular
projects.subtitle: Awarded the most beautiful memory game in class.
projects.short_description: A memory card game built with Angular, with a starry Celest-themed design.
projects.non_technical_description: The classic memory game: flip two cards, remember where they are, and find all the pairs. I gave it a starry, cosmic look, and it was named the most beautiful memory game in my class.
projects.technical_description: Built in one day with Angular. Besides the game logic, the goal was to learn routing between pages and guards that restrict access to some of them.
projects.global_summary: A one-day project to learn Angular's routing and guards, where I also had a lot of fun with the visual side.

projects.title: Todo List
projects.long_title: A Full-Stack Learning Project for Kotlin, Spring Boot, and Vue.js
projects.subtitle: Two weeks of learning new tools from scratch.
projects.short_description: A complete Todo list application built to learn backend/frontend communication with Spring Boot and Vue.
projects.non_technical_description: A simple task manager to add, edit and delete your daily tasks. Nothing fancy on the surface: the real goal was to learn how a front-end and a back-end talk to each other.
projects.technical_description: I used it to learn Kotlin, Spring Boot, PostgreSQL and Vue.js in two weeks. It has REST CRUD endpoints, keeps the front-end in sync with the database, and introduced me to GitHub workflows.
projects.global_summary: A small project, but it's where I learned the basics I still use in every full-stack app.

projects.title: Portfolio v1
projects.subtitle: An early showcase of projects, tutorials, and experiences.
projects.short_description: A first attempt at building a full-stack personal portfolio with CRUD features.
projects.non_technical_description: My very first portfolio, where I gathered my early projects, tutorials and experiences.
projects.technical_description: Built with Kotlin and Spring Boot, Vue.js with Vuetify, and PostgreSQL. The content was managed through CRUD operations, and the backend followed a classic model, repository, DTO and controller structure.
projects.global_summary: Where it all started: my first full-stack project of my own. The portfolio you're reading now is its successor.

comments.title: Portfolio v2
comments.long_title: A Modular and Extensible Next.js Portfolio
comments.subtitle: Built in 1 week — designed for long-term evolution.
comments.short_description: A modern Next.js portfolio with multilingual support, theme context, reusable components, and modular architecture.
comments.non_technical_description: This portfolio represents who I am today, both technically and personally. It adapts easily to new projects and presents my work in a clean and elegant way.
